splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA permits plan actuaries to adopt actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date for withdrawal liability calculations. The timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay, affecting billions of dollars in potential obligations across thousands of multiemployer plans.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the statute does not require actuarial assumptions to be fixed by the measurement date, allowing actuaries flexibility to select assumptions after the end of the prior plan year.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be locked in by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for judicially-created fugitive tolling of supervised release terms, and the period expires as specified in the judgment regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, or whether they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule. The split affects the gatekeeping standards for thousands of federal prisoners seeking post-conviction relief.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, creating an additional hurdle beyond § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy the separate gatekeeping requirements of § 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules like ballot-counting deadlines. The outcome affects whether election-rule disputes are litigated before or after elections, with significant implications for mail-in voting procedures and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election because vote-dilution or competitive injury from allegedly unlawful voting procedures constitutes a cognizable injury in fact.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have standing to challenge election administration rules before an election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized to satisfy Article III requirements.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims in the hospitality and service industry context, leading to inconsistent outcomes. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to clarify standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages applicable to business operators nationwide.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for discrimination claims against business operators, permitting claims based on a wider range of discriminatory conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard for discrimination claims, requiring a higher showing of intentional or systemic discrimination by business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting ambiguous provisions of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of defendants. The split has deepened after the Supreme Court's decisions in Kisor v. Wilkie and Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which narrowed agency deference doctrines.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when Guidelines language is ambiguous, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions even in criminal cases, giving controlling weight to commentary that expands the reach of enhancements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under the First Step Act only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one is disqualifying. The split creates dramatically different sentencing outcomes depending on jurisdiction for defendants with identical criminal histories.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three listed criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) encompasses inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to controlling weight under Stinson, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. The split implicates whether Kisor v. Wilkie limits deference to Guidelines commentary.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative and reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline, so conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Guideline text excludes inchoate offenses; commentary invalid
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously does not include inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, so conspiracy does not qualify as a predicate offense.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. The split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-controlled substance suffices
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state-law offenses regardless of whether the substance is also controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also on the federal controlled substances schedules, because the Guidelines implicitly incorporate the federal definition.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as distinct from the fact or duration of imprisonment) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may bring civil rights claims, and whether habeas jurisdiction extends to BOP decisions regarding First Step Act earned time credits and prerelease custody.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging decisions affecting the execution of their sentences — such as BOP denials of prerelease custody transfers under the First Step Act — or whether such claims may alternatively be brought as civil rights actions. The split affects the procedural vehicles available to thousands of federal prisoners seeking to enforce statutory rights.

positions.label: Habeas is the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim challenges the execution of a sentence and seeks earlier release or transfer to less restrictive custody, habeas corpus under § 2241 is the exclusive or appropriate remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights claims also available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may proceed via civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or § 1983) rather than habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement authorizing such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law — particularly the First Step Act's changes to § 924(c) stacking — can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others defer to the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting consideration of such changes.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly consider punishment as a purpose when revoking supervised release and imposing a sentence, or whether revocation sentences may serve only the limited purposes identified in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may be imposed for punitive purposes. Some circuits allow district courts to expressly punish defendants at revocation, while others hold that the statutory framework limits the purposes of revocation sentences to deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation — excluding retribution.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider punishment as a purpose when imposing a sentence upon revocation of supervised release, permitting express punitive rationales.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that the statutory framework for supervised release revocation excludes retribution/punishment as a permissible sentencing purpose, limiting courts to deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitative goals.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal of a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil appellate deadline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal appellate deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case — triggering the longer civil appeal deadline — or remains part of the criminal case subject to the shorter criminal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion remains part of the criminal proceeding, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtors. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a conflict with circuits that protect debtors' post-petition appreciation upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity are property of the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to debtors
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the estate to property as of the original petition date, meaning post-petition appreciation in equity remains with the debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records in litigation is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order implicating a value of 'high order.'
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, potentially creating a split with circuits that have taken a narrower view of what privacy interests qualify for immediate appeal under Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's stringent requirements, as privacy interests can typically be vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's claim that the BOP violated statutory rights under the First Step Act by denying transfer to prerelease custody based on earned time credits may be brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or must be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement — as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement — are cognizable in habeas corpus or must be brought as civil rights claims. The issue has taken on new importance with First Step Act time-credit claims seeking expedited transfer to halfway houses or home confinement.

positions.label: Habeas corpus is available for such claims
positions.summary: Holds that claims seeking accelerated transfer to prerelease custody based on earned First Step Act time credits affect the duration of confinement and are properly brought as habeas petitions under § 2241.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas corpus is not the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP placement decisions, including transfer to prerelease custody, concern conditions rather than the fact or duration of confinement and should not be brought as habeas petitions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
